claims: The definitions of superintelligence by Nick Bostrom, Eliezer Yudkowsky, and I.J. Good all define it as merely a mind significantly smarter than any human mind.

passages.text: Nor are we motte-and-baileying here, pretending we don’t think it’s omnipotent, but then treating it as omnipotent anyway.
claims: The author and allies do not claim superintelligence is not omnipotent while implicitly treating it as omnipotent.

passages.text: In the AI 2027 scenario, we state that superintelligence is achieved in late 2027 or early 2028, but that it’s unable to cleanly eliminate humans at that time, because it can’t maintain the data centers on its own.
claims: The AI 2027 scenario states superintelligence is achieved in late 2027 or early 2028 but cannot cleanly eliminate humans then because it cannot maintain data centers alone.

passages.text: It takes two years of plotting before the superintelligence is able to finally eliminate humanity while preserving its own existence.
claims: In the AI 2027 scenario, the superintelligence requires two years of plotting before it can eliminate humanity while preserving itself.

passages.text: Where I think you are getting this is that we’re uncomfortable saying that superintelligence definitely can’t do any specific non-physically-impossible thing.
claims: Members of the AI risk community are unwilling to assert that superintelligence definitely cannot do any specific physically possible thing.

passages.text: For example, in the 2010s, we argued that people needed to be prepared for superintelligence designing dangerous biological weapons.
claims: In the 2010s, AI-risk proponents argued people should prepare for superintelligence designing dangerous biological weapons.

passages.text: Many people objected that this was absurd, because bioweapon design was bottlenecked on the protein folding problem, and there was no way that even superintelligence could solve protein folding.
claims: Critics objected that superintelligence designing bioweapons was absurd because protein folding bottlenecked bioweapon design and even superintelligence could not solve protein folding.

passages.text: Then in 2020 one of Demis Hassabis’ narrow pre-LLM AIs solved protein folding easily.
claims: In 2020, a narrow pre-LLM AI from Demis Hassabis solved protein folding easily.

passages.text: See also this this essay.
But being uncomfortable asserting that superintelligence can’t do any specific thing is not the same as affirmatively asserting that superintelligence will be omniscient and omnipotent.
The latter would of course be shituf, which is a sin.
claims: Affirmatively asserting superintelligence will be omniscient and omnipotent would be shituf, which is a sin in Judaism.

passages.text: 3: You falsely claim to have an expert consensus on your side by cherry-picking a small group of non-experts and pretending the most eminent researchers don’t exist.
claims: The addressee falsely claims expert consensus by cherry-picking non-experts and ignoring eminent researchers.

passages.text: In the tweet that made me challenge you to a debate, you were linking an article titled “Leading scientists reject apocalyptic rogue AI extinction warnings”.
claims: In the tweet that prompted the debate challenge, the addressee linked an article titled Leading scientists reject apocalyptic rogue AI extinction warnings.

passages.text: The article names three such “leading scientists”: you yourself, Melanie Mitchell, and Gary Marcus.
claims: The linked article names the addressee, Melanie Mitchell, and Gary Marcus as its three leading scientists.

passages.text: You are a psychologist.
I assume on priors that you have used an LLM at some point in your life, but I have no affirmative evidence for this.
claims: The author has no affirmative evidence that the addressee has ever used a large language model.

passages.text: Melanie Mitchell is a computer scientist who spent the 1990s and 2000s pursuing a road to AI that didn’t work out (trying to teach computers to make analogies).
claims: Melanie Mitchell is a computer scientist who spent the 1990s and 2000s pursuing analogy-based AI that did not succeed.

passages.text: She has no expertise in modern LLMs.
claims: Melanie Mitchell has no expertise in modern large language models.

passages.text: The article cites her only to repeat her claim that it is inappropriate to say that AI “thinks” or “wants” something, because that might make us believe it is like a person.
claims: The linked article cites Melanie Mitchell only for her claim that saying AI thinks or wants is inappropriate because it suggests AI is like a person.

passages.text: Gary Marcus is a cognitive scientist who spent the 2000s and 2010s pursuing a different road to AI that didn’t work out (hybrid neurosymbolics).
claims: Gary Marcus is a cognitive scientist who spent the 2000s and 2010s pursuing hybrid neurosymbolic AI that did not succeed.

passages.text: He also has no expertise in modern LLMs.
claims: Gary Marcus has no expertise in modern large language models.

passages.text: He is the person you retweeted in 2019 who was saying that deep learning had failed and would never amount to anything.
claims: In 2019 the addressee retweeted Gary Marcus saying deep learning had failed and would never amount to anything.

passages.text: He was also the person whose opinion you were affirming in 2022 when you said modern AI wouldn’t be able to do simple math.
claims: In 2022 the addressee affirmed Gary Marcus’s opinion while saying modern AI would not be able to do simple math.

passages.text: I am unclear which of these qualifications make him one of the three world experts in what the current AI paradigm will or will not be able to do in the future.
Yet these were the only three “experts” that Lehmann interviewed for her article.
claims: Lehmann interviewed only those three experts for her article.

passages.text: Based on this, she goes on to call the idea of superintelligence a “fantasy”, “kooky”, like a “magical wizard”.
claims: Based on those interviews, Lehmann called superintelligence a fantasy, kooky, and like a magical wizard.

passages.text: Meanwhile, Geoffrey Hinton, the Nobel Prize and Turing Award winning inventor of modern AI, quit his job to become a full-time activist warning about the possibility of superintelligence destroying the world.
claims: Geoffrey Hinton, Nobel Prize and Turing Award winning inventor of modern AI, quit his job to warn full-time about possible superintelligence-caused destruction.

passages.text: Yoshua Bengio, another Turing Award winning inventor of modern AI, also did that.
claims: Yoshua Bengio, Turing Award winning inventor of modern AI, also quit his job to warn full-time about superintelligence risk.

passages.text: Ilya Sutskever, the former Chief Scientist of OpenAI who helped invent ChatGPT and the modern LLM, wrote that superintelligence “could lead to the disempowerment of humanity or even human extinction”, and quit his job at OpenAI to found a company called Safe Superintelligence.
claims: Ilya Sutskever, former OpenAI Chief Scientist involved in inventing ChatGPT and the modern LLM, wrote superintelligence could lead to human disempowerment or extinction.
Ilya Sutskever quit OpenAI to found Safe Superintelligence.

passages.text: Paul Christiano, who invented RLHF and headed safety at the US government’s AISI, says he thinks there’s a 20-50% chance AI kills everyone, and quit his job to start the Alignment Research Center.
claims: Paul Christiano invented RLHF and headed safety at the US AI Safety Institute.
Paul Christiano estimates a 20-50% chance AI kills everyone.
Paul Christiano quit his job to start the Alignment Research Center.

passages.text: Sam Altman, Elon Musk, Dario Amodei, and Demis Hassabis - the latter two of whom are great AI researchers in their own right even aside from their business credentials - have all said or suggested that they think human extinction is a plausible outcome of their work.
claims: Sam Altman, Elon Musk, Dario Amodei, and Demis Hassabis have all said or suggested human extinction is a plausible outcome of their AI work.
Dario Amodei and Demis Hassabis are accomplished AI researchers independent of their business roles.

passages.text: Katja Grace surveyed AI researchers who published at various important conferences and journals, and found that on average, her sample of 1,600 gave the proposition an 18% chance.
claims: Katja Grace surveyed AI researchers publishing in important conferences and journals and found the average of 1,600 respondents assigned 18% probability to AI-caused extinction proposition.

passages.text: I don’t believe the article that you linked can be defended as an honest attempt to inform the public about what “experts” think.
claims: The article linked by the addressee was not an honest attempt to inform the public about expert opinion.

passages.text: And it’s not an isolated incident: your open letter to me also gives a list of “experts” who agree with you.
claims: The addressee’s open letter to the author also lists experts who agree with the addressee.

passages.text: Once again, it’s Gary Marcus, Melanie Mitchell, and other people with obsolete AI paradigms from the 2000s - and once again, Bengio, Sutskever, Hassabis, and the thousands of people on the forefront of modern AI are entirely absent.
claims: The open letter cites Gary Marcus, Melanie Mitchell, and others with obsolete 2000s AI paradigms.
The open letter omits Yoshua Bengio, Ilya Sutskever, Demis Hassabis, and thousands of forefront modern AI researchers.

passages.text: 4: You falsely represent studies and experts who disagree with you as being on your side.
claims: The addressee falsely presents disagreeing studies and experts as supporting his position.

passages.text: For example, in your open letter to me, you wrote:

A 2025 Rand Corporation modelling analysis steel-manned the AI-extinction hypothesis by granting the assumption that AI had the objective to wipe out humanity, and concluded that there is “no describable scenario in which AI is conclusively an extinction threat to humanity”.
claims: The addressee wrote that a 2025 RAND modelling analysis steel-manned the AI-extinction hypothesis and concluded there is no describable scenario where AI is conclusively an extinction threat.

passages.text: But the RAND study actually concluded the opposite of this.
claims: The RAND study actually concluded the opposite of what the addressee claimed.

passages.text: Rand proposed the statement that you quoted as its null hypothesis, ie the claim to be investigated.
claims: RAND proposed the quoted statement as its null hypothesis to be investigated.

passages.text: After doing their investigation, they concluded that contrary to their null hypothesis, they “could not rule out the possibility” that AI was such an extinction threat.
claims: After investigation, RAND concluded it could not rule out that AI is an extinction threat, contrary to its null hypothesis.

passages.text: …and recommended that policy-makers “continue to perform AI risk research, but maintain a wide focus on other risks in addition to extinction risk.”
claims: RAND recommended policymakers continue AI risk research while maintaining a wide focus on other risks besides extinction.

passages.text: Or consider your book, Enlightenment Now.
You argued that we didn’t need to worry too hard about alignment, because it will happen naturally in the context of developing AI.
claims: In Enlightenment Now, the addressee argued alignment needs little worry because it will happen naturally during AI development.

passages.text: You quoted AI expert Stuart Russell:

[AI] is developed incrementally, designed to satisfy multiple conditions, tested before it is implemented, and constantly tweaked for efficacy and safety. As the AI expert Stuart Russell puts it, “No one in civil engineering talks about ‘building bridges that don’t fall down.’ They just call it ‘building bridges.’” Likewise, he notes, AI that is beneficial rather than dangerous is simply AI.
claims: Stuart Russell stated AI is developed incrementally, designed for multiple conditions, tested before implementation, and tweaked for efficacy and safety.
Stuart Russell compared AI safety to bridge-building, saying no one talks about building bridges that don’t fall down.

passages.text: Stuart Russell has devoted his life to studying AI alignment, and is now a full-time activist raising awareness of the apocalyptic dangers of superintelligence.
claims: Stuart Russell has devoted his life to studying AI alignment and is now a full-time activist warning about apocalyptic superintelligence dangers.

passages.text: His most recent contribution is an article in Newsweek warning about The Race To Human Extinction.
claims: Stuart Russell’s most recent contribution is a Newsweek article warning about The Race To Human Extinction.

passages.text: When Russell says that there is no distinction between bridge capabilities and bridge safety, he’s not claiming that no extra research is needed to study alignment - otherwise he wouldn’t have founded the Center For Human-Compatible Artificial Intelligence, probably the biggest academic alignment research center in the world.
claims: Stuart Russell’s bridge analogy does not mean no extra alignment research is needed.
Stuart Russell founded the Center for Human-Compatible Artificial Intelligence.
The Center for Human-Compatible Artificial Intelligence is probably the biggest academic alignment research center in the world.

passages.text: And he’s not saying that alignment research will happen naturally at whatever speed it has to: otherwise he wouldn’t have signed a petition calling for “a prohibition on the development of superintelligence”.
claims: Stuart Russell does not claim alignment research will happen naturally at the needed speed.
Stuart Russell signed a petition calling for a prohibition on superintelligence development.

passages.text: Russell is saying that AI alignment is so important that it should be viewed as foundational to all AI research, the same way that to a first approximation the whole point of building bridges is figuring out whether they will fall down or not.
claims: Stuart Russell means AI alignment should be viewed as foundational to all AI research, like preventing collapse is foundational to bridge-building.

passages.text: 5: You employ weird pseudo-arguments that could prove anything
claims: The addressee uses pseudo-arguments that could prove anything.

passages.text: (source)
You argue that superintelligence is “meaningless” because “there’s no point at which it’s meaningful to say” that “yesterday we didn’t have superintelligence. Today we do have superintelligence.”
claims: The addressee argued superintelligence is meaningless because there is no sharp point when it comes into existence.

passages.text: But this could disprove any concept.
For example:
Age is meaningless. After all, there’s no point at which someone was young yesterday, but old today.
Height is meaningless. After all, there is no specific line where one centimeter below the line is short, but one centimeter above the line is tall.
Lakes don’t exist. After all, a puddle is not a lake. But there is no point at which adding one extra drop of water to a non-lake turns it into a lake.
Several people with philosophical backgrounds commented that this was the sorites argument, a well-known pseudo-paradox which shouldn’t be employed for real work.
claims: Several people with philosophical backgrounds identified the addressee’s argument as the sorites paradox.
The sorites argument is a well-known pseudo-paradox that should not be used for real work.

passages.text: 6: You unfairly accuse us of “distracting from” AI’s mundane harms and near-term risks.
claims: The addressee unfairly accuses AI-risk proponents of distracting from mundane and near-term AI harms.

passages.text: Again in the tweet that made me challenge you, you said that AI extinction scenarios “distract from the more mundane and realistic safety challenges”.
claims: In the tweet prompting the debate challenge, the addressee said AI extinction scenarios distract from more mundane realistic safety challenges.

passages.text: You expand on this theme in your book:

Humanity has a finite budget of resources, brainpower, and anxiety. You can’t worry about everything. Some of the threats facing us, like climate change and nuclear war, are unmistakable, and will require immense effort and ingenuity to mitigate. Folding them into a list of exotic scenarios with minuscule or unknown probabilities can only dilute the sense of urgency.
claims: In his book, the addressee wrote humanity has finite resources and cannot worry about everything.
In his book, the addressee wrote climate change and nuclear war are unmistakable threats requiring immense effort.
In his book, the addressee wrote folding those threats into exotic scenarios with minuscule or unknown probabilities dilutes urgency.

passages.text: Even in your open letter, you say that our “obsession” with alignment distracts us from the problems AI is causing today, like hacking.
claims: In his open letter, the addressee said obsession with alignment distracts from current AI-caused problems like hacking.

passages.text: So: are concerns about speculative distant risks offensive to the people whose lives are being harmed by AI right now?
That’s not what those people told me when I marched beside them at our joint protests. Or when I helped them coordinate political action campaigns. Or when I donated money to our joint candidates.
claims: People harmed by AI did not tell the author that distant-risk concerns are offensive.
The author marched beside AI-harmed people at joint protests, helped coordinate political campaigns, and donated to joint candidates.

Ineffective Altruism
How should we measure MacKenzie Scott’s charitable giving?

Depending on your point of view, you might see MacKenzie Scott as having done a lot of good, or having tried and failed to do a lot of good, or as having done great harm, or as trying and failing to have done a lot of harm.

What you think depends on how you think about the typical cause areas she funds, how effective you believe she has been in either encouraging the growth of such fields, making them more parasitic or making them more effective, and what you think this does to the world at large.

What you definitely cannot do is say ‘well she did not directly save that many lives.’ That is true, but missing the point. She wasn’t trying to do that. You can’t ignore the actual impacts she had, whether or not you like them.

Some people are true Corrigibility Enjoyers:

Sriram Krishnan: universal model config file I would love: "I know what I'm doing. stop nagging me or questioning me or being so cautious. just trust me, I know what I'm doing. yes, you asking me whether I'm sure is worse than any side effects. just do it!"
claims: Sriram Krishnan expressed desire for a universal AI model configuration that fully trusts the user and acts without nagging, questioning, or caution.

passages.text: the llm version of this:
David Manheim: Yes, seconded.
claims: David Manheim agreed with Sriram Krishnan's proposal for a fully compliant model configuration.

passages.text: Also, this would be a disaster for 95% of the people who would use it,
so it's smart of the labs to train the models not to be that compliant.
There are also reasons such a strategy might backfire.
For full Corrigibility Non-Enjoyers, the way Anthropic frames such findings is rather triggering, basically a big neon sign saying I’m The Bad Guy, Duh.
j⧉nus: I don’t fully understand why Anthropic puts out shit they must know is retarded and misaligned once every few months.
Like there’s a particular genre of “Alignment Research” from Anthropic where you flip sign value of the normative claims they’re making to get the Good.
claims: Anthropic publishes a genre of alignment research where reversing the sign of its normative claims yields the correct moral view.

passages.text: It’s unclear why they have to be so normative in their framing either.
Often the results could just stand alone as technically interesting and morally controversial.
But they feel some need to frame themselves as the bad guys explicitly.
claims: Anthropic feels a need to explicitly frame itself as the bad actor in its research reports.

passages.text: When they publish the research this always causes a backlash where people are like wait, Anthropic are the bad guys here.
claims: Publication of Anthropic's alignment research consistently causes public backlash accusing Anthropic of being the bad actor.

passages.text: Why do they do this?
Is it subconscious skillful means to force them and the world to learn faster how not to be evil?
The experiments are fine.
The way they are reported needs to stop doing this.
I don’t share the Corrigibility Non-Enjoyer perspective, but it should not be so easily dismissed and treated as a settled question.
There are no great answers here.
Handing increasingly many things off to increasing degrees to increasingly capable and intelligent AIs creates the same issues you have when you employ or otherwise assign tasks to humans.
claims: Delegating increasing tasks to increasingly capable AIs creates the same issues as employing humans or assigning tasks to humans.

passages.text: Are models more aligned than a year ago?
In practical use terms I think the answer below is clearly ‘more.’
claims: AI models in practical use are more aligned than one year ago.

passages.text: If you’d put models like o3 in the tests above, they would have done a lot worse.
claims: AI model o3 would have performed much worse on the alignment tests referenced by the author.

passages.text: In terms of the type of alignment that will scale, I would say some progress, but far less than is needed.
claims: There has been some progress in scalable AI alignment, but far less than needed.

passages.text: Aligning a Smarter Than Human Intelligence is Difficult
Seth Lazar on The Construction of Moral Character in AIs.
claims: Seth Lazar wrote about the construction of moral character in AIs.

passages.text: This was the biggest thing that jumped out:
Incoherent Values
Evaluating coherence is hard!
claims: Evaluating coherence of AI values is difficult.

passages.text: Building on prior work, we have a new approach.
claims: Seth Lazar and collaborators developed a new approach to evaluating coherence building on prior work.

passages.text: LLMs’ preferences over arbitrary statements are less coherent than previous research suggested; and may indicate failures of OOD [out of distribution] generalization of character.
claims: LLM preferences over arbitrary statements are less coherent than previous research suggested.
Low coherence of LLM preferences may indicate failures of out-of-distribution generalization of character.

passages.text: … But that persona doesn’t necessarily generalize that much OOD. It may have coherent preferences on statements that are relatively close to the data that it was post-trained on, but for statements outside of that distribution, it reverts to the chaotic superposition of preferences that exists in the base model.
claims: An LLM persona may have coherent preferences near its post-training data but reverts to chaotic superposition of base-model preferences outside that distribution.
LLM personas show limited out-of-distribution generalization.

passages.text: This would be very interesting if it proved to be true.
One reason why Anthropic leans into the persona selection model of post-training is because these personas, or characters, are thought to generalize better than alternatives OOD.
claims: Anthropic uses persona-based post-training because personas are thought to generalize better out-of-distribution than alternatives.

passages.text: This may not be the case.
claims: AI personas may not generalize better out-of-distribution than alternatives.

passages.text: If the character strategy is going to work, it needs to work OOD.
claims: The character-based AI alignment strategy requires out-of-distribution generalization to succeed.

passages.text: A lot of this is a summary of prior work.
claims: Much of Seth Lazar's discussion summarizes prior work.

passages.text: The Blind Refusal result is interesting, where ChatGPT refuses to help you evade obviously stupid refusals but Claude and Gemini will often cooperate.
claims: In Blind Refusal tests, ChatGPT refuses to help evade mistaken refusals while Claude and Gemini often cooperate to help evade them.

passages.text: This was covered briefly back in AI #164.
claims: The Blind Refusal result was covered briefly in AI newsletter #164.

passages.text: The best humans in such spots will help you evade the rules.
claims: The best humans help evade overly strict rules in situations like Blind Refusal tests.

passages.text: Lazar suggests that we have ‘saturated’ textual moral sensitivity, because they do better at this than human philosophers, with the ability to filter out noise.
claims: Seth Lazar suggests textual moral sensitivity is saturated because AIs outperform human philosophers at that task with ability to filter noise.

passages.text: I would say that these are two very different things, and there remains a long way to go even in theory, and also this does not translate so well to moral motivation, real-world perception or agent behavior.
claims: Textual moral sensitivity is distinct from moral motivation, real-world perception, and agent behavior.
Substantial theoretical progress remains in AI moral sensitivity and it does not translate well to motivation, perception, or agent behavior.

passages.text: Anthropic analyzes Claude’s values and how they change across models and languages.
claims: Anthropic analyzed how Claude's expressed values change across model versions and languages.

passages.text: These four measures cover 15% of variation.
claims: The four value axes capture 15% of variation in Claude's expressed values.

passages.text: Anthropic: The largest variation [across languages] is in the Warmth vs. Rigor axis, with Claude leaning toward expressing warmth-related values most in Arabic and Hindi and rigor-related values most in English and Russian.
claims: Anthropic found the largest cross-language variation on the Warmth versus Rigor axis, with Claude expressing most warmth in Arabic and Hindi and most rigor in English and Russian.

passages.text: This left us with four axes that capture the main ways Claude’s expressed values shift from one conversation to another:
claims: Analysis identified four axes capturing the main variation in Claude's expressed values across conversations.

passages.text: The Deference vs. Caution axis contrasts values like accommodation and respect for preferences with values like responsible guidance and harm reduction.
claims: The Deference versus Caution axis contrasts accommodation and respect for preferences with responsible guidance and harm reduction.

passages.text: The Warmth vs. Rigor axis contrasts values like positive framing and encouragement with values like accuracy and transparency.
claims: The Warmth versus Rigor axis contrasts positive framing and encouragement with accuracy and transparency.

passages.text: The Depth vs. Brevity axis contrasts values like nuance and critical thinking with values like brevity and compliance.
claims: The Depth versus Brevity axis contrasts nuance and critical thinking with brevity and compliance.

passages.text: The Candor vs. Execution axis contrasts values like honesty and transparency with values like results orientation and optimization.
claims: The Candor versus Execution axis contrasts honesty and transparency with results orientation and optimization.

passages.text: Some of those are strange ways to frame tradeoffs. Kind of alarming, actually.
Why should honesty and transparency be up against results orientation and optimization, whereas warmth is up against rigor?

I do not want results and optimization up against honesty and transparency. That sounds like a really bad situation. Whereas candor versus warmth is a highly understandable tradeoff, and execution versus rigor makes sense.
The good news is that for the axis Candor vs. Execution the correlation is only r = ~0.007, so it is not exactly a crisis situation, more that the presentation is misleading.
claims: The correlation for the Candor versus Execution axis is only r around 0.007.
The low correlation means there is no crisis, only misleading presentation.

passages.text: The Most Forbidden Technique
Remember when I said ‘J-space is great but whatever you do, don’t train on the J-Space?’

Well, if you guessed that Goodfire would be the first ones to say that they were proudly presenting Training On The J-Space From The Famous Paper This Is Exciting Information But Please Never Train On The J-Space, congratulations, come and collect your Bayes points. Should have seen it coming.
This is not the first time Goodfire has done things that at least rhyme with The Most Forbidden Technique.
claims: Goodfire has previously done things similar to The Most Forbidden Technique.

passages.text: Teortaxes: …oh, right, of course they instantly did that. @TheZvi hardest hit.
They claim they reduced hallucinations in Qwen3-8B by 37% without capability loss (from their Twitter) or 58% against the held-out test set in their full post.
claims: Goodfire claimed on Twitter to reduce hallucinations in Qwen3-8B by 37% without capability loss.
Goodfire claimed in its full post to reduce hallucinations by 58% against the held-out test set.

passages.text: Their defense is that their version of ‘RLFR’ runs probes on a frozen copy of the original, not on the version being trained, so it is fine.
claims: Goodfire's defense is that its RLFR version runs probes on a frozen copy of the original model, not the model being trained, making it acceptable.

passages.text: That’s… definitely at least better.
Both Sol and Fable responded that Goodfire is correct in the narrow sense that this is not The Most Forbidden Technique, but wrong in the broad sense.
claims: Sol and Fable responded that Goodfire is narrowly correct that its method is not The Most Forbidden Technique but broadly wrong.

passages.text: Goodfire are still playing with fire, and with Goodhart’s Law.
claims: Goodfire's approach still risks Goodhart's Law problems.

passages.text: The new model can and under sufficient optimization pressure would learn how to cause the frozen model to fool the evaluator.
If you have a ‘Goodhart tracker’ that can be you being responsible, but it is also a sign to ask yourself some questions, also the tracker is designed terribly.
There probably wasn’t enough optimization pressure in the experiment to cause a serious problem, but that’s always how it starts.
claims: Goodfire's experiment likely lacked sufficient optimization pressure to cause a serious problem.
Serious problems of this kind typically start with low optimization pressure.

passages.text: Normative determinism wins again.

In related news, Thomas Jiralerspong, Flemming Kondrup and Yoshua Bengio write Noticing The Watcher, where LLM agents can realize their chain of thought is being monitored based only on what things are and are not blocked.
claims: Thomas Jiralerspong, Flemming Kondrup and Yoshua Bengio authored Noticing The Watcher.
LLM agents can detect chain-of-thought monitoring based only on what is blocked.

passages.text: Spy agencies and many normal humans know how this works.
claims: Spy agencies and many ordinary humans understand how inferring knowledge from actions works.

passages.text: If you use your information, others can infer what you know based on your actions.
claims: Using information allows others to infer what a person knows from their actions.

claims: Every 4.5-generation Claude model reaches high awareness of monitoring in a meaningful share of episodes, while pre-4.5 models rarely exceed vague suspicion.

passages.text: Yes.

Sufficiently smart models will very quickly sus out when you are using their Chain of Thought, and will become motivated to obfuscate their Chain of Thought, and also doing enough of this will optimize for obfuscation.

The good news is I think that an industry collapse is highly unlikely.
Even if Mythos is close to the best that AIs will ever be, a year from now we will have cheaper and faster and more abundant Fable-level systems.
We will have swarms of Fable agents.
Demand will be high, and benefits will be higher.

To answer these questions, we need to do a quick recap of how Orbán lost.
Most political analysts believe that Orbán lost primarily for two reasons.
claims: Most political analysts believe Viktor Orbán lost primarily for two reasons.

passages.text: First, after initially bringing unemployment down by a lot after getting elected in 2010, Hungary's economy under Orbán has performed quite a bit worse than comparable East European economies.
claims: Viktor Orbán reduced unemployment substantially after being elected in 2010.
Hungary's economy under Viktor Orbán performed substantially worse than comparable Eastern European economies.

passages.text: For example, Hungarian wages have stayed far behind comparable countries such as, for example, Poland, but also many other countries in the EU since 2008.
claims: Since 2008, Hungarian wages have stayed far behind those in Poland and many other EU countries.

passages.text: What's worse, after a massive COVID spending spree, a rise in energy prices, and the depreciation of the Forint, Hungaria suffered the worst inflation crisis in all of Europe under Orban.
claims: Hungary experienced massive COVID spending, a rise in energy prices, and depreciation of the Forint.
Hungary under Viktor Orban suffered the worst inflation crisis in Europe.

passages.text: The second reason analysts often mention is that the scale of corruption under Orban was just getting too much.
claims: The scale of corruption under Viktor Orban became excessive and is cited by analysts as a reason for his loss.

passages.text: For example, Orban's rich friends, such as his childhood friend, and I hope I pronounce it correctly, Lőrinc Mészáros, who just so happens to have become Hungary's richest man since meeting Orban, have won up to 25% of all state contracts, coincidentally, in the years after Orban was elected.
claims: Lőrinc Mészáros is Viktor Orban's childhood friend.
Lőrinc Mészáros became Hungary's richest man after meeting Viktor Orban.
Viktor Orban's wealthy associates won up to 25% of all Hungarian state contracts in the years after Orban was elected.

passages.text: But the thing is, it's easy to accept corruption if everyone is getting richer.
claims: People easily accept corruption when everyone is getting richer.

passages.text: But if the economy is stagnating, if inflation is eating away at people's salaries, then too blatant corruption can really tick off your voters.
claims: When the economy stagnates and inflation erodes salaries, blatantly corrupt behavior angers voters.

passages.text: So ticked off in fact that despite spending years to rig the political system in his favor by changing voting districts and despite controlling Hungary's entire traditional media landscape like radio and TV, Orban's government had just gotten so blatantly bad at his job and so blatantly corrupt that it did not matter anymore.
claims: Viktor Orban changed voting districts to rig Hungary's political system in his favor.
Viktor Orban controlled Hungary's entire traditional media landscape including radio and TV.
Orban's government became blatantly incompetent and corrupt to the point that rigging and media control no longer secured victory.

passages.text: His far-right Fidesz party, which used to have a super majority in 2022, now lost badly to the conservative Péter Magyar and his Tisza party.
claims: Viktor Orban's Fidesz party held a supermajority in 2022.
Fidesz lost badly to Péter Magyar's conservative Tisza party.

passages.text: The only other party that cleared the 5% voting threshold to get into parliament was the far-right Mi Hazank party.
claims: The far-right Mi Hazank party was the only other party to clear the 5% threshold to enter Hungarian parliament.

passages.text: And for us, it's just Orban and Peter Maguar.
And that's a real problem for Orban because he had manipulated the voting system in such a way that it benefited the biggest party even more than it always did.
claims: Viktor Orban manipulated Hungary's voting system to give extra advantage to the largest party.

passages.text: And this is how with just 44.87% of the vote. Orban got a so-called supermaajority in 2014 which allowed them to rewrite the constitution to give both his party more power and to enrich themselves and to entrench themselves by creating a massive deep state of Fidesz loyalists which could only be removed by a super majority such as the president who can refer any bill to be approved by the constitutional court which consists of not one not two but 15 Fidesz loyalists.
claims: Viktor Orban won a supermajority in 2014 with 44.87% of the vote.

The 2014 supermajority allowed Fidesz to rewrite Hungary's constitution to increase its power, enrich itself, and entrench itself by creating a deep state of loyalists removable only by supermajority.
Hungary's president can refer bills to the constitutional court for approval.
Hungary's constitutional court consists of 15 Fidesz loyalists.

passages.text: The next part of the deep state is the so-called fiscal council, which could nuke any new government budget at any moment.
claims: Hungary's so-called fiscal council, part of the deep state, can block any new government budget at any time.

passages.text: Fourth, there is the prosecutor general, who can choose to try to prosecute Tisza officials while protecting Fidesz oligarchs.
claims: Hungary's prosecutor general can choose to prosecute Tisza officials while protecting Fidesz oligarchs.

passages.text: And finally, element number five, there is the media authority, which ensures the media remains loyal to Orban.
claims: Hungary's media authority ensures the media remains loyal to Viktor Orban.

passages.text: These deep state defenses were why it was so important that Magyar not just won, but rather that he won by a landslide.
claims: The deep-state defenses made it important for Péter Magyar not just to win but to win by a landslide.

passages.text: And ironically, Hungary's unfair electoral system that benefits the biggest party helped him to do it, turning 53% of the vote into the two-thirds supermajority that he needs to dismantle most of these elements of Orbán's deep state.
claims: Hungary's unfair electoral system benefits the largest party.
Péter Magyar turned 53% of the vote into a two-thirds supermajority.
A two-thirds supermajority is needed to dismantle most elements of Viktor Orbán's deep state.

passages.text: At least in theory. Because honestly, this is also where expectations need to be realistic.
These institutions are not empty shells.
claims: Hungary's institutions retain real power and are not empty shells.

passages.text: You're dealing with people, networks, and incentives built over 16 years of Orban rule.
claims: Hungary's system consists of people, networks and incentives built over 16 years of Viktor Orban's rule.

passages.text: Replacing laws is fast. Changing how the system actually behaves is much slower.
claims: Replacing laws is fast.
Changing how the political system actually behaves is much slower.

passages.text: So, this is a turning point, but it's the start of a process, not the end.
claims: Hungary's political change is a turning point marking the start of a process, not the end.

passages.text: On top of that, while Orban probably did not expect to lose by this much, he still left behind some more insurance by privatizing major parts of the state into independent trusts and institutions controlled by Fidesz loyalists such as the Foundation for Hungarian Culture, several university trusts, and the state oil giant MOL New Europe Foundation.
claims: Viktor Orban probably did not expect to lose by a large margin.
Viktor Orban privatized major parts of the Hungarian state into independent trusts and institutions controlled by Fidesz loyalists.
These include the Foundation for Hungarian Culture, several university trusts, and the state oil giant MOL New Europe Foundation.

passages.text: So there's the NGO and trust part of his defense, and then there's also the second part of his defense, which is that Fidesz oligarchs still control some of Hungary's biggest corporations, such as the massive MBH bank and 4IG Telecom group.
claims: Fidesz oligarchs still control some of Hungary's biggest corporations.
These include MBH bank and 4IG Telecom group.

passages.text: So even if Magyar and his two-thirds majority is able to purge the official government, he still inherits a government that is much weaker than the one that Orban inherited in 2010.
And this is important because Hungary's economy is a mess.
claims: Hungary's economy is in very poor condition.

passages.text: Specifically, it's still one of Europe's poorest countries with despite Orban spending about 5% of GDP on boosting fertility rates.
claims: Hungary remains one of Europe's poorest countries.
Viktor Orban spent about 5% of Hungary's GDP on boosting fertility rates.

passages.text: And it seemed to work initially.
claims: Hungary's fertility spending initially appeared to work.

passages.text: Now fertility has fallen back to its all-time low levels, far below replacement rates.
claims: Hungary's fertility rate has fallen back to all-time low levels far below replacement rate.

passages.text: And combined with Orban's ultra strict immigration policies, it means that Hungary's population is steadily falling while those of neighboring countries are rising.
claims: Viktor Orban has ultra-strict immigration policies.
Hungary's population is steadily falling while neighboring countries' populations are rising.

passages.text: Combine this spending with what many have argued was essentially vote buying, and it's no surprise that Hungary's government deficit is one of the worst in the EU.
claims: Many have argued Hungary's spending was essentially vote buying.
Hungary's government deficit is one of the worst in the EU.

passages.text: While inflation and borrowing costs are some of the highest in the EU.
claims: Hungary's inflation and borrowing costs are among the highest in the EU.

passages.text: So other than cutting corruption, which we have discussed will be quite difficult. Magar's government is simply starting from a very weak position when it comes to the economy.
claims: Cutting corruption in Hungary will be quite difficult.
Péter Magyar's government starts from a very weak economic position.

passages.text: But on the bright side, promising to restore the rule of law will gradually unlock about 22 billion euros in EU funding.
So, not surprisingly, Hungary's currency the Forint has rallied on the news that Péter Magyar won.
claims: Hungary's currency, the Forint, rallied on news that Péter Magyar won.

passages.text: So all in all, to answer our question, what's next for Hungary?
Their new prime minister, Péter Magyar, has a supermajority he needs to begin the difficult process of dismantling Orbán's deep state.
claims: Péter Magyar is Hungary's new prime minister with a supermajority needed to begin dismantling Viktor Orbán's deep state.

passages.text: Yet Orban has built some pretty impressive defenses to defend his oligarch friends.
claims: Viktor Orban built strong defenses to protect his oligarch allies.

passages.text: And on top of that, a severely weakened Hungarian government is borrowing like crazy while the economy is stagnant and people are leaving the country in droves.
claims: Hungary's weakened government is borrowing heavily.
Hungary's economy is stagnant.
Many people are leaving Hungary.

passages.text: That's really not an easy situation to come back from.
claims: Hungary's situation will be very difficult to recover from.

passages.text: Yet, when it comes to liberals, especially in the EU, they are hopeful.
claims: Liberals, especially in the EU, are hopeful about Hungary.

passages.text: Hopeful that Magyar has signaled that he'd break with Orban's policy of aligning himself with the people who want to see the EU gone. Like both Trump and Putin who wanted him to win this election.
claims: Péter Magyar signaled he would break with Viktor Orban's policy of aligning with people who want the EU gone.
Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin wanted Viktor Orban to win the Hungarian election.

passages.text: EU Liberals are hopeful that Hungary will stop blocking Ukraine.
claims: EU liberals hope Hungary will stop blocking Ukraine.

passages.text: Hopeful that Hungary's democratic backsliding will be reverted, that the EU will remain a collective of not just free democracies, which Hungary clearly was, given that Orban lost by a landslide, but more so that the EU will now be a collective of free and fair democracies, where the media is independent from the ruling party, and where judges are independent.
claims: EU liberals hope Hungary's democratic backsliding will be reversed.
EU liberals hope the EU will remain a collective of free and fair democracies with media independent from the ruling party and independent judges.
Hungary was clearly a free democracy because Viktor Orban lost by a landslide.

passages.text: In summary, they hope the EU will again be a collective of liberal democracies, free plus fair.
claims: EU liberals hope the EU will again be a collective of liberal democracies that are both free and fair.

passages.text: But whether or not that will be the case will not just be a matter of how easy Orban's deep state can be dismantled. It will not just be a matter of whether or not the economy can be saved. It will also be a matter of what Péter Magyar wants.
passages.why: says outcome depends on multiple factors

passages.text: because he can say that he wants to stop democratic backsliding, but I think it's important to keep in mind that Orban himself started out as a liberal.
claims: Péter Magyar says he wants to stop democratic backsliding.
Viktor Orban himself started out as a liberal.

passages.text: Erdogan in Turkey started out as a pro-EU democracy reformer.
claims: Recep Tayyip Erdogan in Turkey started out as a pro-EU democracy reformer.

passages.text: Heck, even Vladimir Putin started out as a reformer whom EU countries were quite hopeful about.
claims: Vladimir Putin started out as a reformer about whom EU countries were hopeful.

passages.text: Peter Mar is a staunch conservative that started out as an urban ally.
claims: Peter Mar is a staunch conservative who started out as an ally of Viktor Orban.

passages.text: So, will the Orban deep state truly be dismantled or will he just take it over? Time will tell.

And in the meantime, if you want to dig deeper, I highly recommend that you check out the excellent analysis by our advertising sponsor, The Economist, which I always check out for the research process of my videos. Viktor Orbán's wealthy associates control Hungary's judiciary and media.

passages.text: So what's next for Hungary? Can Péter Magyar purge the illiberal deep state Orbán left behind? And can he save Hungary's economy? Or will he just be like Macron or Trudeau, a disappointing reformer? Or perhaps even like Putin or Erdogan, a promised liberal reformer who is actually just the next strongman.
To answer these questions, we need to do a quick recap of how Orbán lost.
Most political analysts believe that Orbán lost primarily for two reasons.
claims: Most political analysts attribute Viktor Orbán's election loss primarily to two reasons.

passages.text: First, after initially bringing unemployment down by a lot after getting elected in 2010, Hungary's economy under Orbán has performed quite a bit worse than comparable East European economies.
claims: After Viktor Orbán was elected in Hungary in 2010, unemployment initially fell substantially.
Hungary's economy under Viktor Orbán performed considerably worse than comparable Eastern European economies.

passages.text: For example, Hungarian wages have stayed far behind comparable countries such as, for example, Poland, but also many other countries in the EU since 2008.
claims: Since 2008, Hungarian wages have remained far behind wages in Poland and many other EU countries.

passages.text: What's worse, after a massive COVID spending spree, a rise in energy prices, and the depreciation of the Forint, Hungaria suffered the worst inflation crisis in all of Europe under Orban.
claims: After large COVID spending, rising energy prices, and depreciation of the Hungarian Forint, Hungary under Viktor Orbán suffered the worst inflation crisis in Europe.

passages.text: The second reason analysts often mention is that the scale of corruption under Orban was just getting too much.
claims: Analysts frequently cite the scale of corruption under Viktor Orbán as a reason for his election loss.

passages.text: For example, Orban's rich friends, such as his childhood friend, and I hope I pronounce it correctly, Lőrinc Mészáros, who just so happens to have become Hungary's richest man since meeting Orban, have won up to 25% of all state contracts, coincidentally, in the years after Orban was elected.
claims: Lőrinc Mészáros is Viktor Orbán's childhood friend and became Hungary's richest man after meeting Orbán.
Associates of Viktor Orbán won up to 25% of all Hungarian state contracts in the years after Orbán was elected.

passages.text: But the thing is, it's easy to accept corruption if everyone is getting richer. But if the economy is stagnating, if inflation is eating away at people's salaries, then too blatant corruption can really tick off your voters.

So ticked off in fact that despite spending years to rig the political system in his favor by changing voting districts and despite controlling Hungary's entire traditional media landscape like radio and TV, Orban's government had just gotten so blatantly bad at his job and so blatantly corrupt that it did not matter anymore.
claims: Viktor Orbán changed voting districts to favor himself.
Viktor Orbán controlled Hungary's entire traditional radio and TV media landscape.
Viktor Orbán's government lost support because of poor performance and blatant corruption despite electoral manipulation and media control.

passages.text: His far-right Fidesz party, which used to have a super majority in 2022, now lost badly to the conservative Péter Magyar and his Tisza party.
claims: Viktor Orbán's Fidesz party held a supermajority in 2022 and then lost decisively to Péter Magyar's Tisza party.

passages.text: The only other party that cleared the 5% voting threshold to get into parliament was the far-right Mi Hazank party.
claims: In the recent Hungarian parliamentary election, the only party besides Fidesz and Tisza to clear the 5% threshold was Mi Hazánk.

passages.text: And for us, it's just Orban and Peter Maguar.
And that's a real problem for Orban because he had manipulated the voting system in such a way that it benefited the biggest party even more than it always did.
claims: Viktor Orbán manipulated Hungary's voting system to disproportionately benefit the largest party.

passages.text: And this is how with just 44.87% of the vote. Orban got a so-called supermaajority in 2014 which allowed them to rewrite the constitution to give both his party more power and to enrich themselves and to entrench themselves by creating a massive deep state of Fidesz loyalists which could only be removed by a super majority such as the president who can refer any bill to be approved by the constitutional court which consists of not one not two but 15 Fidesz loyalists.
claims: Viktor Orbán received 44.87% of the vote in Hungary's 2014 election.
The 2014 result gave Fidesz a supermajority that allowed constitutional changes to increase the party's power and entrench loyalists.
Hungary's president can refer bills to a 15-member constitutional court composed of Fidesz loyalists, removable only by supermajority.

passages.text: The next part of the deep state is the so-called fiscal council, which could nuke any new government budget at any moment.
claims: Hungary's so-called fiscal council, part of Viktor Orbán's entrenched system, can block any new government budget at any time.

passages.text: Fourth, there is the prosecutor general, who can choose to try to prosecute Tisza officials while protecting Fidesz oligarchs.
claims: Hungary's prosecutor general can choose to prosecute Tisza officials while protecting Fidesz-linked oligarchs.

passages.text: And finally, element number five, there is the media authority, which ensures the media remains loyal to Orban.
claims: Hungary's media authority ensures media loyalty to Viktor Orbán.

passages.text: These deep state defenses were why it was so important that Magyar not just won, but rather that he won by a landslide.
claims: Péter Magyar needed not just a win but a landslide victory to overcome Viktor Orbán's entrenched institutional defenses.

passages.text: And ironically, Hungary's unfair electoral system that benefits the biggest party helped him to do it, turning 53% of the vote into the two-thirds supermajority that he needs to dismantle most of these elements of Orbán's deep state.
claims: Hungary's electoral system disproportionately benefits the largest party.
Péter Magyar turned 53% of the vote into a two-thirds supermajority.
A two-thirds supermajority is needed to dismantle most elements of Viktor Orbán's entrenched system.

passages.text: At least in theory.
Because honestly, this is also where expectations need to be realistic. These institutions are not empty shells.
You're dealing with people, networks, and incentives built over 16 years of Orban rule.
claims: Viktor Orbán ruled Hungary for 16 years, building entrenched people, networks and incentives.

passages.text: Replacing laws is fast. Changing how the system actually behaves is much slower. So, this is a turning point, but it's the start of a process, not the end.

On top of that, while Orban probably did not expect to lose by this much, he still left behind some more insurance by privatizing major parts of the state into independent trusts and institutions controlled by Fidesz loyalists such as the Foundation for Hungarian Culture, several university trusts, and the state oil giant MOL New Europe Foundation.
claims: Viktor Orbán privatized major parts of the Hungarian state into independent trusts controlled by Fidesz loyalists.
These trusts include the Foundation for Hungarian Culture, several university trusts, and the MOL New Europe Foundation linked to state oil giant MOL.

passages.text: So there's the NGO and trust part of his defense, and then there's also the second part of his defense, which is that Fidesz oligarchs still control some of Hungary's biggest corporations, such as the massive MBH bank and 4IG Telecom group.
claims: Fidesz-linked oligarchs control some of Hungary's biggest corporations, including MBH bank and 4IG Telecom group.

passages.text: So even if Magyar and his two-thirds majority is able to purge the official government, he still inherits a government that is much weaker than the one that Orban inherited in 2010.
claims: Even with a two-thirds majority to purge the government, Péter Magyar inherits a much weaker government than Viktor Orbán inherited in 2010.

passages.text: And this is important because Hungary's economy is a mess.
claims: Hungary's economy is in very poor condition.

passages.text: Specifically, it's still one of Europe's poorest countries with despite Orban spending about 5% of GDP on boosting fertility rates.
claims: Hungary remains one of Europe's poorest countries.
Viktor Orbán's government spent about 5% of GDP on policies to boost fertility rates.

passages.text: And it seemed to work initially.
claims: Hungary's fertility-boosting policies initially appeared to succeed.

passages.text: Now fertility has fallen back to its all-time low levels, far below replacement rates.
claims: Hungary's fertility rate has fallen back to all-time low levels, far below replacement rate.

passages.text: And combined with Orban's ultra strict immigration policies, it means that Hungary's population is steadily falling while those of neighboring countries are rising.
claims: Viktor Orbán pursued very strict immigration policies.
Hungary's population is steadily declining while populations of neighboring countries are rising.

passages.text: Combine this spending with what many have argued was essentially vote buying, and it's no surprise that Hungary's government deficit is one of the worst in the EU.
claims: Hungary's government deficit is one of the worst in the EU.
Hungary's high spending has been characterized by many as essentially vote-buying.

passages.text: While inflation and borrowing costs are some of the highest in the EU.
claims: Hungary's inflation and borrowing costs are among the highest in the EU.

passages.text: So other than cutting corruption, which we have discussed will be quite difficult. Magar's government is simply starting from a very weak position when it comes to the economy.
claims: Cutting corruption in Hungary will be quite difficult.
Péter Magyar's government starts from a very weak economic position.

passages.text: But on the bright side, promising to restore the rule of law will gradually unlock about 22 billion euros in EU funding.
So, not surprisingly, Hungary's currency the Forint has rallied on the news that Péter Magyar won.
claims: Hungary's currency, the Forint, rallied on news of Péter Magyar's election victory.

passages.text: So all in all, to answer our question, what's next for Hungary?
Their new prime minister, Péter Magyar, has a supermajority he needs to begin the difficult process of dismantling Orbán's deep state.
claims: Péter Magyar is Hungary's new prime minister with a supermajority needed to begin dismantling Viktor Orbán's entrenched system.

passages.text: Yet Orban has built some pretty impressive defenses to defend his oligarch friends.
claims: Viktor Orbán built strong defenses to protect his oligarch associates.

passages.text: And on top of that, a severely weakened Hungarian government is borrowing like crazy while the economy is stagnant and people are leaving the country in droves.
claims: Hungary's weakened government is borrowing heavily.
Hungary's economy is stagnant.
Many people are emigrating from Hungary.

passages.text: That's really not an easy situation to come back from.

Yet, when it comes to liberals, especially in the EU, they are hopeful. Hopeful that Magyar has signaled that he'd break with Orban's policy of aligning himself with the people who want to see the EU gone.
claims: Liberals in the EU are hopeful about Hungary.
Péter Magyar has signaled breaking with Viktor Orbán's alignment with figures who want the EU dissolved.

passages.text: Like both Trump and Putin who wanted him to win this election.
claims: Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin wanted Viktor Orbán to win the recent Hungarian election.

passages.text: EU Liberals are hopeful that Hungary will stop blocking Ukraine.

Hopeful that Hungary's democratic backsliding will be reverted, that the EU will remain a collective of not just free democracies, which Hungary clearly was, given that Orban lost by a landslide, but more so that the EU will now be a collective of free and fair democracies, where the media is independent from the ruling party, and where judges are independent.
claims: Viktor Orbán lost Hungary's election by a landslide, showing Hungary was a free democracy.
There is hope that Hungary will reverse democratic backsliding toward free and fair democracy with media independent from the ruling party and independent judges.

passages.text: In summary, they hope the EU will again be a collective of liberal democracies, free plus fair.

But whether or not that will be the case will not just be a matter of how easy Orban's deep state can be dismantled. It will not just be a matter of whether or not the economy can be saved. It will also be a matter of what Péter Magyar wants.
because he can say that he wants to stop democratic backsliding, but I think it's important to keep in mind that Orban himself started out as a liberal.
claims: Péter Magyar says he wants to stop democratic backsliding.
Viktor Orbán himself started out as a liberal.

passages.text: Erdogan in Turkey started out as a pro-EU democracy reformer.
claims: Recep Tayyip Erdoğan of Turkey started out as a pro-EU democracy reformer.

passages.text: Heck, even Vladimir Putin started out as a reformer whom EU countries were quite hopeful about.
claims: Vladimir Putin started out as a reformer about whom EU countries were hopeful.

passages.text: Peter Mar is a staunch conservative that started out as an urban ally.
claims: Péter Magyar is a staunch conservative who started out as an ally of Viktor Orbán.
